clue.text: Architect's the latest to design number 16

indicators.note: the latest letter of a word is its final one, so take the end of design

parts.note: points to the answer at 16 across, a tree giving these three letters

explanation.surface: An architect is said to be the newest to design a building numbered sixteen.
explanation.walkthrough: 'number 16' is a cross-reference: the solver uses the answer to 16 across.
explanation.definitionFit: John Nash was the Regency architect behind Regent Street and the Brighton Pavilion.

clue.text: Various such types here joined in French course

parts.note: the French word for in is en
the grid is full of kinds of tree, so the type here is a tree

explanation.surface: Assorted types of people have joined a French course.
explanation.walkthrough: 'such types here' refers to the puzzle's theme: many answers are trees.
explanation.definitionFit: An entrée is a dish served as a course of a meal, a main course in the US.

clue.text: Bondgirl's outside occasionally nude

indicators.note: the outside of a word is its first and last letters, here those of girl
taking letters only now and then means every other one of nude

explanation.surface: A Bond girl is pictured, now and then, in the nude.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bondgirl's' reads as the film heroine, but Bond is the definition, split off from girl's.
explanation.definitionFit: Glue is an adhesive, and a bond is what sticks two things together.

clue.text: Brian, coming from Spanish mountains, volunteers a song

indicators.note: the name Brian departs from the mountain range's name, leaving the rest behind

parts.note: the Cantabrian Mountains run across northern Spain
taken as written
TA is the Territorial Army, Britain's volunteer reserve

explanation.surface: A man called Brian, fresh from Spain's mountains, offers to sing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Brian' looks like the subject of the sentence; he is the letters removed from CANTABRIAN, leaving CANTA.
explanation.definitionFit: A cantata is a vocal composition for singers with instruments, so loosely a song.

clue.text: Chap with origins in Crumpsall or Chorlton?

definitions.text: Chap with origins in Crumpsall or Chorlton?

parts.note: a chap is a man

indicators.note: the origin of a word is its first letter, shared by both place names

explanation.surface: A man whose roots lie in Crumpsall or Chorlton, two districts of Manchester.
explanation.walkthrough: Crumpsall and Chorlton are districts of Manchester; both begin with C, which follows MAN.
explanation.definitionFit: Manc is informal British slang for a person from Manchester, a Mancunian.

clue.text: Son and husband respectively leave meal hurt, seeing human body part

indicators.note: the letters for son and husband go away from the two words that follow

parts.note: supper is an evening meal

indicators.note: pairs the second letter with the second word, so husband's letter leaves hurt

parts.note: to hurt is to harm

explanation.surface: A son and husband each walk out of a meal, hurt, having seen a body part.
explanation.walkthrough: 'respectively' pairs Son with meal and husband with hurt: S leaves SUPPER, H leaves HARM.
explanation.definitionFit: The upper arm is the part of the human limb between shoulder and elbow.

clue.text: A Bow Street resident inside is planning to catch these?

definitions.text: A Bow Street resident inside is planning to catch these?

parts.note: the indefinite article can be an as well as a
an arch is a bow shape

indicators.note: something resident inside another lives within it, so the street's letters sit within is

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A Bow Street officer inside is plotting to catch some anarchists.
explanation.walkthrough: Bow Street in London was home to the Bow Street Runners, an early police force, and a famous magistrates' court.
explanation.definitionFit: Anarchists, who reject all government, were the target of Victorian policing plans.

clue.text: Feel unwell playing sport briefly turning purplish

indicators.note: turning a sequence round means reading the letters from the back

parts.note: to ail is to feel unwell
a show that is playing is on

indicators.note: said briefly, the word loses its last letter

parts.note: a game is a sport

explanation.walkthrough: 'turning' sends AILONGAM backwards; 'briefly' trims GAME to GAM.
explanation.definitionFit: Magnolia flowers range into pinkish purple, so the shade is a fair colour sense here.

clue.text: A pound gains entry to slopes in ski resort

parts.note: a pound is an enclosure for animals, a pen

indicators.note: the entry to a word is its opening letter, here of slopes

explanation.walkthrough: 'pound' looks like money; it is an animal enclosure, a PEN.
explanation.definitionFit: Aspen in Colorado is a famous skiing destination, also the name of a poplar tree.

clue.text: Tree camouflaged the masked thief, out of bounds unseen

indicators.note: something camouflaged has its look disguised, so these letters appear rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: the out-of-bounds letters become invisible, dropped from the thief

parts.note: a masked thief is a robber

explanation.surface: A tree hid a masked thief who stayed out of sight beyond the boundary.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tree' is not a plant but the actor Herbert Beerbohm Tree; THE plus RBER (ROBBER without OB) is rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Sir Herbert Beerbohm Tree was a celebrated Victorian actor-manager, so Tree is his surname.

clue.text: Cricket ball caught by slip-up in Headingley, just edging…

parts.note: C is the cricket scorecard abbreviation for caught

indicators.note: the slip-up sits within the edges of the ground's name
only the edge letters, first and last, of Headingley are used

parts.note: to slip up is to err

explanation.surface: A catch off a nick at Headingley cricket ground, the ball just edged.
explanation.walkthrough: Headingley is a Test cricket ground in Leeds; its edge letters H and Y hold ERR.
explanation.definitionFit: A cherry is cricket slang for a new red ball, from its shiny colour.

clue.text: …long leg close to rope

parts.note: pins is slang for legs, so a leg is a pin

indicators.note: the close of a word is its last letter, here of rope

explanation.surface: Continuing the cricket scene: the fielder at long leg stands close to the boundary rope.
explanation.walkthrough: Long leg is a fielding position near the boundary rope; here 'long' is the definition and 'leg' is wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: To pine is to long for something, yearning for what is absent.

clue.text: PR person, self-proclaimed treasure and playboy, top to bottom?

parts.note: someone calling themself a treasure says I'm a gem

indicators.note: in a down entry the top letter of the playboy goes to the bottom

parts.note: a rake is a dissolute playboy

explanation.walkthrough: 'top to bottom' moves R from the head of RAKE to its foot, giving AKER.
explanation.definitionFit: An image-maker is someone who shapes a public image, like a public relations specialist.

clue.text: Car collection that's across the pond

parts.note: a lot is a group of items at auction, a collection
across the pond, the Atlantic, from Britain is the USA, abbreviated US

explanation.surface: A car collection that is kept in America.
explanation.walkthrough: Lotus is a British sports-car maker.
explanation.definitionFit: Lotus is a make of British sports car, so it can be called a car.

clue.text: Officer circling agreed with second-in-command to bring ship to rest

indicators.note: the officer's letters go round the agreeing word

parts.note: LT is the abbreviation for lieutenant, an officer
ay or aye means yes, agreed

indicators.note: second in a word means its second letter, here of command

explanation.surface: An officer, with his deputy's agreement, brings the ship to a halt.
explanation.walkthrough: 'second-in-command' looks like a deputy; it means the second letter of command, O.
explanation.definitionFit: To lay to is a nautical phrase for stopping a vessel, holding it head to wind.

clue.text: Battle to get criminal out of the soup?

indicators.note: the criminal is got out of the soup, removed from its letters

parts.note: consommé is a clear soup
a con is a convict, a criminal

explanation.surface: A struggle to get a crook out of trouble, being in the soup.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in the soup' means in trouble, but here the soup is CONSOMME.
explanation.definitionFit: The Somme was a First World War battle of 1916 in northern France.

clue.text: Cockney's hotpot remains

indicators.note: a Cockney speaker drops the aitch at the start of words

parts.note: a hash is a stew of chopped meat, like a hotpot

explanation.surface: The leftovers of a Cockney's stew.
explanation.walkthrough: Cockneys, working-class Londoners, famously drop initial H, so HASH loses it.
explanation.definitionFit: Ash is what remains after burning, as in a person's cremated remains.

clue.text: Household wing accommodates French friend

indicators.note: to accommodate a guest is to house them within

parts.note: to wing it is to fly
ami is French for friend

explanation.surface: One wing of the house has room for a friend from France.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wing' looks like part of a building; it is the verb, to FLY.
explanation.definitionFit: A household is the people living together under one roof, typically a related group.

clue.text: After shin injured, Manchester United player's ruined

indicators.note: an injured body part is damaged, so the letters are knocked out of order

parts.note: Manchester United are nicknamed the Red Devils, so a player is a Red, plus the 's

explanation.surface: After a shin injury, a Manchester United footballer's season is wrecked.
explanation.walkthrough: Manchester United are an English football club; their players are the Reds.
explanation.definitionFit: Something torn to shreds is wrecked beyond repair, ruined.

clue.text: Mike has money saved to cover flash cocktail

parts.note: Mike is M in the radio alphabet

indicators.note: the savings account wraps round the flash

in a flash means a moment, a mo

explanation.walkthrough: 'flash' looks like an adjective, showy; it is a moment, MO.
explanation.definitionFit: A mimosa is a drink of champagne and orange juice, much like a Buck's Fizz.

clue.text: Chess writer, master peripherally in charge during match

indicators.note: these letters fall within the match, set inside its letters

explanation.walkthrough: 'Chess' is not the board game but the 1980s musical, whose lyrics Tim Rice wrote.
explanation.definitionFit: Sir Tim Rice wrote the lyrics for the musical Chess with Benny and Björn of ABBA.

clue.text: Golfer periodically missing sulked going round

indicators.note: going round means turning back the way it came
every other letter of sulked goes missing, leaving the odd ones

explanation.surface: A golfer who keeps missing putts sulks his way round the course.
explanation.walkthrough: The odd letters of sulked give SLE, which 'going round' turns about.
explanation.definitionFit: Ernie Els is a South African golfer and multiple major champion.

clue.text: Female crew inspired by encouraging cry

explanation.walkthrough: 'crew' is a rowing four, shown as the Roman numeral IV.
explanation.definitionFit: Olive is a woman's first name, so it can define a female.

clue.text: Hearts of heroic losers lifted

indicators.note: the heart of each word is its central pair of letters

explanation.definitionFit: Rose is the past tense of rise, so it can mean went up, lifted.

clue.text: Son probing ancestry finds where people settled?

explanation.walkthrough: A roost is where birds settle for the night; the question mark flags applying it to people.
explanation.definitionFit: Roosts are perches where birds settle, here jokingly places where people settled down.

clue.text: Old comic accepted participating in draw at end of festival

explanation.walkthrough: 'draw' looks like a raffle; it is the verb to LURE.
explanation.definitionFit: Stan Laurel was the thin half of the classic comedy double act Laurel and Hardy.

clue.text: Play about English poet, not popular

indicators.note: the popular word is not there, removed from the poet

parts.note: Philip Larkin was an English poet
something popular is in

explanation.walkthrough: 'Play about' looks like a drama on a subject; it is the verb, to fool around.
explanation.definitionFit: To lark about is to fool around, play about mischievously.

clue.text: Tory MP reportedly studied material for cabinet

clue.text: Churchman always embraces Lord first and last

clue.text: Jumper perhaps that might cover such teachers
